"A 67 year old patient presented to clinic requesting a septoplasty. He had an incidental finding of a deviated nasal septum on imaging — and the moment he became aware of it, he was convinced he needed surgery. The challenge was that he had absolutely no breathing complaints, no functional symptoms whatsoever.

I was present during the encounter, and it was the resident who took the lead. What struck me was how difficult it was to redirect the patient — he kept coming back to the fact that the deviation was there, visible and documented, and in his mind that meant it needed to be fixed.

Watching how the resident handled it taught me a great deal. He listened fully, acknowledged the patient's concern, and then walked him through the reasoning clearly — that we do not operate on findings, we operate on patients. A deviation without symptoms in a 67 year old carries real surgical risk with no real benefit.

By the end of the consultation the patient understood, and they reached a shared decision together. That encounter stayed with me — because it showed me that sometimes the best thing you can do for a patient is protect them from an operation they do not need."

The transition from medical student to intern is one of the most sudden shifts you will ever experience in medicine. One day you are an observer — watching, learning, standing at the periphery. The next day you are part of the team, and the weight of that responsibility lands on you before you feel ready for it.

But what I learned is that the difficulty of that transition is precisely the point. It is in those early uncomfortable months that you discover what you are actually made of — how you handle uncertainty, how you communicate under pressure, how you show up for your team even when you are exhausted.

And when that moment finally comes — when you realize you are no longer just watching but genuinely contributing — it is one of the best feelings medicine has to offer.

"During one of my clinic rotations, a patient presented with a complaint of hearing his own voice when speaking — autophony — along with intermittent popping sounds in his ear. Honestly, my first thought was Eustachian tube dysfunction, but I could not piece together the full picture.

The resident came in, asked me to present the case, and then asked the patient what seemed like a completely random question — 'Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?'

The patient paused, surprised, and confirmed that yes — he had lost a considerable amount of weight in a short period of time.

The resident explained that rapid weight loss can cause loss of the peripharyngeal fat pad that normally keeps the Eustachian tube closed — leading to a patulous Eustachian tube, where the tube stays abnormally open. That was the cause of everything the patient had been experiencing.

What made this case stay with me was not just the diagnosis — it was the patient's reaction. He said that he had been to multiple clinics and no one had ever connected his symptoms to his weight loss. In that one question, the resident gave him an explanation that finally made sense of months of frustration.

That moment taught me that a thorough history is not just about systems — it is about seeing the whole person in front of you."

Q: Last non-medical book you read?

"I've always been drawn to fiction that keeps you thinking. Recently I finished Inferno by Louise Cooper — part of a fantasy series. Before that I've gone through Dan Brown's series, Agatha Christie's The Man in the Brown Suit, J.K. Rowling's The Cuckoo's Calling, and Jeffrey Archer's Only Time Will Tell. I tend to gravitate toward stories built around mystery, strategy, and characters who operate under pressure 



"I've always made time for reading outside medicine — I tend to gravitate toward mystery, strategy, and characters under pressure:"

  • Inferno – Louise Cooper — Fantasy series. A woman cursed to hunt demons she herself unleashed. About owning your mistakes and relentlessly correcting them. She can never rest until every demon is recaptured.
  • Dan Brown – Robert Langdon Series — A Harvard symbologist racing through art, history and conspiracy across Europe. In Inferno specifically, Langdon fails to stop the virus — it's already released — but it turns out to be a sterilizing agent, not a killer. Ends on a moral dilemma, not a clean win.
  • Agatha Christie – The Man in the Brown Suit — A bored young woman witnesses a suspicious death in London and follows the trail to South Africa. Christie's classic trick: the villain is the charming aristocrat hiding in plain sight the whole time.
  • J.K. Rowling – The Cuckoo's Calling — A broke war-veteran detective hired to prove a supermodel was murdered. The twist: the client who hired him is the killer.
  • Jeffrey Archer – Only Time Will Tell — A dock worker's son rising through 1920s England trying to uncover who his father really was. Ends on a deliberate cliffhanger — the question is never answered in Book 1.

CHUNK 1 — WHO I AM (10 seconds) "My name is Yahya Samman. I'm 25, born and raised in Jeddah — a KSAU-HS alumnus, graduated valedictorian, first in my class, with a GPA of 4.98."


CHUNK 2 — WHY ENT 

WHY ENT I was seriously considering neurosurgery for most of medical school — the complexity drew me in. But when I got to the wards, I realized the scope was narrow, the prognosis was heavy, and the day-to-day left little room for the kind of diverse, evolving practice I wanted. ENT was the complete opposite. It's surgical and medical. The skill set never stops growing — microsurgery, endoscopy, head and neck oncology, rehabilitation. The patient population spans every age. The subspecialties are deep enough to spend a career in any one of them. And the prognosis — you actually see people recover, hear, breathe, speak again. No other specialty gave me that combination. ENT was the only one where I genuinely lost track of time.

- I also have a passion for building things. In my free time I build personal productivity tools and automate my own workflow using AI — I currently have a working AI-powered personal assistant I built from scratch. 

- And I train as much as I can . 


I'm here because I want to train at the highest level — and I've spent six years making sure I'd be ready."

🧭 Principle Patient safety is the highest priority — but my response has to be proportional to the risk. Not every lapse carries the same urgency.

🔵 Before First — I check myself. Am I certain this is poor care, or is there clinical reasoning beyond my current level of knowledge? I acknowledge my limits as a resident. There are decisions that look wrong from the outside that make complete sense with more context.

🟢 Now I triage the situation immediately:

Is this life-threatening? → I escalate right now. No private conversation first, no waiting. I go to the highest available authority and I document everything in real time. The patient's life comes before anyone's comfort.

Is this suboptimal but not immediately dangerous? → I approach the consultant privately and respectfully — framing it as seeking understanding, not accusation. "I wanted to clarify the plan for this patient — I may be missing something." That gives them room to correct course with dignity. If they dismiss me and I'm still certain — I escalate.

🟡 Later
